notes.gr-sva:
Only a handful of questions per paper, but zero ambiguity once you know the rules — reliably free marks

The verb must agree in number with its true subject — the trap is almost always that something sits between subject and verb, or the "obvious" word isn't the real subject at all.

Rules that cover most CUET questions

Subject patternVerb
Two subjects joined by andplural — Ram and Shyam are here
Two subjects joined by or / nor / either...or / neither...noragrees with the nearer subject — either she or her daughters have made this
Indefinite pronouns — each, every, either, neither, everyone, anybodyalways singular, even before a plural-looking phrase
None of + plural nounusually plural in modern usage — none of the boys have attended
Some/all/most/a lot of + nounagrees with the noun after of — plural noun → plural verb
Collective nouns (team, family, committee)singular when acting as one unit; plural when members act individually
A phrase between subject and verb (along with, as well as, together with)ignored — verb still agrees with the original subject
A relative clause subject (who, which, that)agrees with whatever the pronoun refers back to

Method

  1. Cross out everything between the subject and the verb — a prepositional phrase or "as well as" clause never changes the verb.
  2. Find the TRUE subject, not the nearest noun — it may be several words earlier.
  3. For or/nor subjects, the verb only ever matches the subject closest to it.
  4. For a relative clause ("who were invited"), trace who/which/that back to its real antecedent before deciding singular or plural.

⚠ Common traps

  • A long phrase between subject and verb disguises which noun is really governing the verb.
  • "None" and collective nouns can genuinely take either singular or plural depending on context — CUET's official answer key generally prefers plural with 'none of + plural noun'.
  • In an either...or sentence, students default to matching the FIRST subject instead of the nearer one.
  • A relative clause's verb has to match the antecedent, not the immediately preceding word.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Cross out the interrupting phrase

'None of the boys _____ attended the party.' Choose: had not / has / have / are.

1

Identify what sits between subject and verb: 'of the boys' — a prepositional phrase, doesn't change the core subject.

2

The core subject is 'none', referring back to a plural group ('the boys').

3

Modern usage (and CUET's own answer key) treats 'none of + plural noun' as taking a plural verb.

Answer: Have — 'none of the boys have attended' is the real CUET answer.

Method 2 — Nearer-subject rule for either/or

'Either Savita or her daughter _____ made this delicious pudding.' Choose: was / have / is / has.

1

Identify the two subjects joined by 'either...or': 'Savita' (singular) and 'her daughter' (singular).

2

The verb agrees with whichever subject is nearer to it — here, 'her daughter', which is singular.

3

A singular subject in this context (present perfect) takes 'has', not 'have'.

Answer: Has — agrees with the nearer subject 'her daughter', both singular.

Method 3 — A relative-clause subject

'Some of the people _____ to the party can't come.' Choose: invites / inviting / who were invited / they were invited.

1

Notice the blank isn't the main verb of the sentence — the main verb is 'can't come', later on.

2

The blank needs a relative clause modifying 'the people' — describing WHICH people, using who/which/that.

3

'invites' and 'inviting' aren't grammatical here; 'they were invited' repeats the subject instead of using a relative pronoun.

Answer: Who were invited — the only option that correctly forms a relative clause describing 'the people'.
notes.gr-tenses:
≈4 questions per paper — mostly about picking the right tense from time-clues in the sentence, not naming tenses

CUET rarely asks you to name a tense — it asks you to pick the correct verb form for a sentence, using time-clue words and the relationship between two clauses (which happened first) as the evidence.

The tense families

AspectSimpleContinuousPerfectPerfect continuous
PresentI writeI am writingI have writtenI have been writing
PastI wroteI was writingI had writtenI had been writing
FutureI will writeI will be writingI will have writtenI will have been writing

Sequence-of-tense — the real CUET skill

When a sentence has two events at different points in the past, the EARLIER one takes past perfect, and the LATER one takes simple past — this single rule solves most CUET tense questions with two clauses.

By the time we arrived, the concert _____ and the crowd _____ in the parking lot.

Two past events: the concert ending and the crowd gathering both happened before "we arrived" (itself already past). Both earlier events need past perfect.

Real CUET answer: had already ended, had gathered.

Time-signal words and the tense they demand

Signal wordTense it usually forces
yesterday, last week, in 2020simple past
since, for (with 'have')present/past perfect
by the time, before, after (two past events)past perfect for the earlier one
when + past simple, interrupting an ongoing actionpast continuous for the ongoing action
never... before, already, justpresent/past perfect

Method

  1. Find every time-signal word in the sentence first — they usually settle the tense outright.
  2. If two past events are compared, decide which happened first — that one takes past perfect.
  3. For an action interrupted by another ("when the Principal entered, a student ___ on the blackboard"), the ongoing action takes past continuous.
  4. Check subject-verb agreement matches whatever tense you've chosen.

⚠ Common traps

  • Two past events in one sentence, but only simple past used for both — loses the 'which happened first' information CUET is testing.
  • 'Since' vs 'for' — since + a point in time, for + a duration; both usually pair with a perfect tense, not simple past.
  • An interrupted past action written in simple past instead of past continuous.
  • Present tense used for a general/habitual truth, tested as if it needed present continuous instead ("these grapes ___ sour" = simple present, a stated fact/quality, not an ongoing action).

Worked methods

Method 1 — Which event happened first?

'By the time we arrived, the concert _____ and the crowd _____ in the parking lot.' Choose: has ended,was gathering / had already ended,had gathered / ended,gather / was ending,gathered.

1

Identify the reference point: 'we arrived' — simple past.

2

Both the concert ending and the crowd gathering happened BEFORE we arrived — they're earlier than an already-past event.

3

An event earlier than another past event takes past perfect, not simple past.

Answer: Had already ended, had gathered — both earlier-past events correctly marked with past perfect.

Method 2 — An interrupted action

'When the Principal entered the class, a student _____ on the blackboard.' Choose: wrote / writes / is writing / was writing.

1

Identify the interrupting event: 'the Principal entered' — a single, simple-past action.

2

The writing was already in progress WHEN that happened — an ongoing action interrupted by a shorter one.

3

An ongoing past action takes past continuous, not simple past.

Answer: Was writing — the ongoing action interrupted by the Principal's entrance.

Method 3 — A stated fact/quality, not an action in progress

'These grapes _____ sour in comparison to what I had yesterday.' Choose: is tasting / taste / tasted / have tasted.

1

Notice 'taste' here describes a quality of the grapes (how they ARE), not an action being performed.

2

Verbs describing states/qualities (taste, seem, feel used this way) stay in simple present even when other 'continuous-looking' options are offered.

3

Reject 'is tasting' — that would mean someone is actively tasting them right now, which isn't what the sentence means.

Answer: Taste — a state/quality verb stays simple present; 'is tasting' wrongly implies an ongoing action of tasting.
notes.gr-articles:
≈3 questions per paper — a/an/the plus the wider family of determiners (each, few, some, both)

CUET tests both the three articles (a / an / the) and the broader class of determiners — each, every, some, any, few, a few, both — that also sit in front of nouns and are easy to confuse with each other.

a / an / the — the core rules

RuleExample
a before a consonant SOUNDa university (starts with a 'yoo' sound)
an before a vowel SOUNDan hour (the h is silent)
the for something specific/already knownthe lion is the king of beasts (a whole class, treated as one known thing)
No article for general plural/uncountable nounslions are dangerous (no 'the')
Repeated a/an before each noun in a comparisona better statesman than a philosopher — not 'a...philosopher' alone

Determiners that recur

DeterminerUse
each / everysingular noun, singular verb — 'each section will contain 20 students'
a few / few'a few' = some (positive); 'few' = almost none (negative)
some / any'some' in positive statements/offers; 'any' in negatives/questions
bothexactly two, always plural verb
little / a littleuncountable-noun equivalent of few/a few

Method

  1. Decide sound, not spelling, for a/an — "an hour" (silent h), "a university" (yoo- sound despite the vowel letter).
  2. For a comparison ("a better X than a Y"), repeat the article before BOTH nouns being compared — dropping the second is a very common CUET distractor.
  3. For each/every, check the verb stays singular even if the surrounding sentence describes a group.
  4. For few vs a few, decide if the sentence's tone is "not much, unfortunately" (few) or "some, and that's fine" (a few).

⚠ Common traps

  • Judging a/an by the letter instead of the sound — 'an hour' but 'a university'.
  • Dropping the second article in a comparison: 'a better statesman than philosopher' is wrong; needs 'than a philosopher'.
  • 'The' used for a general plural class where no article is needed, or omitted where a specific single thing needs 'the'.
  • Few/a few and little/a little swapped — they're near-opposites in tone despite looking almost identical.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Repeat the article in a comparison

'He would make a better statesman than _____ university professor.' Choose: a / the / an / a,a.

1

Notice this is a comparison between two roles: statesman and university professor.

2

English requires the article repeated before the second noun in this kind of comparison too.

3

Between 'a' and 'an', decide by sound: 'university' starts with a 'yoo-' consonant sound, so it takes 'a', not 'an'.

Answer: A, a — 'a better statesman than a university professor', both by sound and by the repeated-article rule.

Method 2 — the whole-class 'the'

'_____ lion is _____ king of beasts.' Choose: a,the / the,the / a,an / the,a.

1

Recognise 'lion' here means the whole species treated as one known category, not one random lion — this needs 'the', not 'a'.

2

'King of beasts' is a specific, unique title — also takes 'the', not 'a'.

Answer: The, the — both nouns are being treated as specific/unique, not as one example among many.

Method 3 — each vs a few

'The class will be divided into three sections and _____ section will contain 20 students.' Choose: each / every / both / all of the above.

1

Notice the sentence is talking about the sections individually, one at a time ('will contain 20 students' — describing each section's own count).

2

'Each' is used when treating members of a group one by one, especially right after they've been introduced as a set (here, 'three sections').

3

'Every' is more general/habitual in tone; 'both' only works for exactly two — there are three sections here, ruling it out.

Answer: Each — used for treating the three sections individually, right after they've been introduced as a specific set.
notes.gr-prepositions:
≈7 questions per paper — one of the highest-yield Grammar sub-topics. Fixed collocations, not logic, decide the answer

Prepositions attach to specific verbs, adjectives, and nouns by convention — "afraid of", "depend on", "married to" — not by any rule you can reason out. CUET tests both filling the right preposition and spotting a wrong one already in a sentence.

High-frequency preposition collocations

WordCorrect preposition
afraidof
depend / dependenton
marriedto
indebtedto (a person), for (a thing)
proudof
angrywith (a person), at (a situation)
interestedin
good / badat (a skill)
differentfrom
similarto
arriveat/in (never 'arrive to')
returnhome (no preposition), to (a place)

Prepositions of place, time and movement

TypeExamples
Place (fixed point vs surface vs enclosed)at the corner · on the table · in the box
Timeat 5 o'clock · on Monday · in July
Movement through/acrossacross the field, through the forest, along the road
Method/meansby car, by hand, with a knife

Method

  1. For fill-in-the-blank, identify the fixed word before the blank (afraid/depend/married/etc.) — the preposition is locked to that word, not to logic.
  2. For "spot the incorrect usage", check each option's verb/adjective + preposition pairing against the collocation list, not against what "sounds okay" in isolation.
  3. "The kite is flying on the sky" is wrong not because of grammar theory, but because English simply says "flying in the sky" — memorise the pairing.

⚠ Common traps

  • A preposition that would work with a DIFFERENT verb gets planted for the actual verb in the sentence.
  • "Return home" takes NO preposition at all — 'returned to home' is a common wrong-option trap.
  • Two-preposition pairs tested in one sentence ("across... through") — both need to be individually correct, not just one.
  • "By" (method) vs "in" vs "with" confused for transport/means — 'by car' not 'in car', 'by hand' not 'with hand'.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Lock the preposition to the fixed word

'She is standing_____her husband in this crisis.' Choose: with / in / for / by.

1

The idiom here is 'stand by someone' = support them, not literally stand next to them.

2

This is a fixed collocation, not a logical choice — 'stand with' sounds plausible but isn't the tested idiom.

Answer: By — 'stand by' is the fixed idiom meaning to support someone.

Method 2 — Two prepositions, both must be right

'The hikers walked _____ the open field and then made their way _____ the dense forest.' Choose: along,over / around,under / into,beside / across,through.

1

Check the first blank: crossing an open field surface → 'across'.

2

Check the second blank: moving through the middle of a forest, not around it → 'through'.

3

Reject any option where only one of the two blanks is right — both need to be correct together.

Answer: Across, through — the field is crossed (across), the forest is moved through the middle of (through).

Method 3 — Spot the incorrect usage

Choose the sentence that uses the preposition incorrectly: 'Read the poem on page 50' / 'I live on street 10' / 'The kite is flying on the sky' / 'Put on your new clothes.'

1

Check each against its fixed collocation: 'on page 50' ✓, 'on street 10' ✓ (a fixed usage for addresses), 'put on clothes' ✓ (phrasal verb).

2

'Flying on the sky' breaks the fixed pairing — English says 'flying IN the sky', treating the sky as an enclosing space, not a surface.

Answer: The kite is flying on the sky — should be 'in the sky'.
notes.gr-pronouns:
A small handful of questions per paper — mostly relative pronouns (who/whom/whose/which/that) and possessives

CUET's pronoun questions cluster around picking the right relative pronoun to introduce a clause, and around possessive-pronoun spelling (a classic apostrophe trap).

Relative pronouns — which one, when

PronounUse
whosubject of the clause, refers to a person — 'the man who called'
whomobject of the clause, refers to a person — 'the man whom I met'
whosepossession — 'a friend whose brother is a doctor'
whichrefers to a thing/animal — 'the book which I read'
thatperson or thing, in defining clauses only — no comma before it

Possessive pronouns — no apostrophe, ever

CorrectNever
yoursyour's
hersher's
theirstheir's
its (possession)it's (that always means 'it is')

Method

  1. Decide if the pronoun's antecedent is a person or a thing — that alone eliminates half the options (who/whom/whose vs which).
  2. For who vs whom, check whether the pronoun is doing the action (who) or receiving it (whom) inside its own clause.
  3. For "whose", check that the sentence is expressing possession/belonging, not just a relationship in general.
  4. Never add an apostrophe to a possessive pronoun — that spelling always signals a contraction (it's = it is), never possession.

⚠ Common traps

  • 'Which' used for a person instead of 'who'.
  • An apostrophe added to a possessive pronoun (your's, her's, their's) — none of these exist in standard English.
  • 'Its' vs "it's" — the single most common CUET/competitive-exam pronoun trap.
  • 'Whose' used where the sentence needs 'who' (no possession involved) or vice versa.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Possession needs 'whose'

'Mohan has a friend _____ brother is a doctor.' Choose: which / who / that / whose.

1

Check what relationship is being expressed: the friend's brother — possession/belonging.

2

Only 'whose' expresses possession among the options; who/that/which don't.

Answer: Whose — expresses that the brother belongs to (is related to) the friend.

Method 2 — Subject role needs 'who', not 'whom'

'The students _____ came late to the class have missed out on some important concepts.' Choose: who / which / whom / whose.

1

Find the verb inside the relative clause: 'came late' — someone is doing this action.

2

The pronoun is the SUBJECT of 'came late' (the one doing the coming), not an object.

3

A subject pronoun referring to people is 'who', not 'whom' (object) or 'which' (things).

Answer: Who — subject of 'came late', referring to people.

Method 3 — Possessive pronoun, no apostrophe

'In a formal letter we write _____ sincerely.' Choose: Your / your's / yours / you.

1

Identify this needs a possessive pronoun standing alone (not before a noun) — the standard sign-off phrase.

2

'Your' needs a noun after it (your letter); it can't stand alone.

3

Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe — eliminate "your's" immediately.

Answer: Yours — the correct standalone possessive pronoun, no apostrophe.
notes.gr-adj-adv:
≈3–4 questions per paper — choosing the right adverb by meaning, and spotting words that work as both adjective and adverb

Most CUET adjective/adverb questions are really vocabulary-in-a-grammar-wrapper — pick the adverb whose meaning fits the sentence — plus a recurring trick: a handful of English words are identical in their adjective and adverb forms.

Words that are both adjective AND adverb, unchanged

WordAs adjectiveAs adverb
fasta fast carrun fast (not 'run fastly')
harda hard questionwork hard (not 'work hardly')
wella well person (healthy)she sings well
latea late trainarrived late
earlyan early startwoke up early

Note: "hardly" and "lately" DO exist, but mean something different — hardly = barely/almost not; lately = recently. They are not the "-ly" version of hard/late.

Common adverbs by the meaning they add

FunctionExamples
Manner (how)slowly, carefully, eagerly
Degree (how much)highly, barely, merely, extremely
Time/frequencydaily, rarely, often, already
Sentence adverbs (comment on the whole sentence)unfortunately, surprisingly, credibly

Method

  1. For a vocabulary-style blank ("_____, he thinks too highly of himself"), read the whole sentence for tone before picking an adverb — the answer usually needs to logically connect to the rest of the sentence.
  2. For "which of these is NOT an adverb" questions, check each word's actual job in a sentence — a word ending in -y isn't automatically an adjective (greedy is), and a word without -ly isn't automatically not an adverb (scarce/scarcely — note "scarce" itself is an adjective, "scarcely" is the adverb).
  3. For "convert -ing clause to adjective + infinitive", keep the meaning identical while changing only the grammatical form.

⚠ Common traps

  • Assuming every '-ly' word is an adverb and every non-'-ly' word is an adjective — many common adverbs have no -ly (fast, hard, well, late).
  • 'Hardly'/'lately' mistaken for the adverb forms of 'hard'/'late' — they mean something else entirely.
  • Degree adverbs with opposite-strength near-twins planted together (barely/merely/hardly = weak; highly/greatly = strong).
  • A comparative or superlative adjective used where a plain adverb was needed, or vice versa.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Pick the adverb that fits the sentence's logic

'Although she had initial doubts about the project, it eventually turned out to be _____ successful.' Choose: barely / merely / hardly / highly.

1

Note the contrast set up by 'although... eventually' — doubts at first, but a strong positive outcome later.

2

'Barely', 'merely', and 'hardly' are all weak-intensity words — they'd contradict the positive turn the sentence describes.

3

Only 'highly' matches a genuinely successful, strong outcome.

Answer: Highly — the only strong-intensity option, matching the sentence's positive turn.

Method 2 — Words that are both adjective and adverb

Choose a word that can be used as an adjective as well as an adverb, unchanged: good / well / hand / hardly.

1

Test each in both roles: 'good' is only an adjective (a good book); the adverb form is 'well', not 'good'.

2

'Well' works both ways: 'a well person' (adjective, healthy) and 'she sings well' (adverb).

3

'Hand' isn't an adverb at all; 'hardly' is only an adverb, with its own distinct meaning (barely).

Answer: Well — functions as both an adjective (healthy) and an adverb (in a good manner), unchanged.

Method 3 — Identifying which words are NOT adverbs

Which of the given words are NOT adverbs: A. Already B. Greedy C. Certainly D. Scarce E. often.

1

Check each word's actual job: 'already' (time), 'certainly' (degree/sentence adverb), 'often' (frequency) — all genuine adverbs.

2

'Greedy' describes a noun's quality directly ('a greedy man') — it's an adjective, not an adverb.

3

'Scarce' also describes a noun ('scarce resources') — it's an adjective; the adverb form is 'scarcely'.

Answer: B and D only — Greedy and Scarce are adjectives, not adverbs.
notes.gr-conjunctions:
≈2 questions per paper — connecting logic words, plus identifying adjective clauses (a recurring real-paper pattern)

CUET tests conjunctions two ways: picking the connector whose LOGIC fits the sentence (contrast, cause, time), and — a pattern that shows up often in real papers — identifying or building an adjective clause (a relative clause that describes a noun, introduced by who/which/whose/that).

Conjunctions by the logic they signal

LogicConjunctions
Additionand, moreover, furthermore
Contrast (same clause)but, yet, whereas, although, though
Contrast (strong, unexpected)nevertheless, however
Cause / reasonbecause, since, as
Resultso, therefore, consequently
Timewhen, while, before, after, as soon as, until
Conditionif, unless, provided that

Adjective clauses — a distinct, recurring CUET pattern

An adjective clause is a relative clause (starting with who/which/whose/that/where) that describes a noun just before it — it functions AS an adjective for that noun, even though it's a full clause.

"A man whose habits are industrious is sure to succeed."

The clause "whose habits are industrious" describes the noun "a man" — that whole clause is the adjective clause.

Method

  1. For a fill-in-the-blank connector, identify the LOGICAL relationship between the two halves of the sentence first (is it a contrast? a result? a time sequence?), then pick the matching conjunction — not just whichever "sounds smooth".
  2. To spot an adjective clause, find a relative pronoun (who/which/whose/that/where) and check whether the clause it starts is describing a specific noun right before it.
  3. Distinguish a genuine adjective clause from a clause playing a different role (noun clause, adverb clause) — an adjective clause always attaches to and describes one specific noun.

⚠ Common traps

  • A mild contrast word ("although") used where the sentence actually needs a strong, unexpected-contrast word ("nevertheless") or vice versa.
  • "Whereas" and "although" both signal contrast but aren't always interchangeable in a fixed sentence structure.
  • A clause that looks like it starts with a relative pronoun but is actually a noun clause (answering "what", not describing a noun) — mistaken for an adjective clause.
  • Options built from unrelated grammar errors mixed in alongside the real adjective-clause option, to test if you can actually spot the clause type, not just eliminate obviously broken sentences.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Match the logic, not just the vibe

'He is a miser _____ he spent lakhs on his daughter's marriage.' Choose: therefore / although / whereas / nevertheless.

1

Identify the logical relationship: being a miser (stingy) directly CONTRADICTS spending lakhs — a strong, surprising contrast.

2

'Whereas' sets up a contrast between two different subjects being compared, not a surprising contradiction about the SAME subject — doesn't fit here.

3

'Although' would need to come at the start, restructuring the sentence — as a mid-sentence connector here it doesn't fit the sentence's given shape as cleanly as a strong contrast marker.

4

'Nevertheless' signals exactly this: despite being a miser, he still spent lavishly — a strong, unexpected contrast.

Answer: Nevertheless — signals the surprising contradiction between being a miser and spending lakhs.

Method 2 — Spotting the adjective clause

Identify the adjective clause: 'A man whose habits are industrious is sure to succeed.'

1

Find the relative pronoun: 'whose'.

2

Check what noun it's describing: 'a man' — the clause describes what kind of man.

3

The full clause starting at the relative pronoun and describing that noun is the adjective clause.

Answer: Whose habits are industrious — describes 'a man', functioning as an adjective clause.

Method 3 — Choosing the sentence WITH an adjective clause

Choose the sentence that has an Adjective Clause: 'I expect to get a prize' / 'He laughs best who laughs last' / 'He confessed to his guilt' / 'You may sit wherever you like'.

1

Check each option for a relative pronoun attached to and describing a specific noun.

2

'I expect to get a prize' and 'He confessed to his guilt' have no relative clause at all.

3

'You may sit wherever you like' — 'wherever' introduces an adverb clause of place, not an adjective clause (it doesn't describe a noun).

4

'He laughs best who laughs last' — 'who laughs last' describes 'he' (the implied subject/person), functioning as an adjective clause.

Answer: He laughs best who laughs last — the only option containing a genuine adjective clause.
notes.gr-modals:
≈4 questions per paper — each modal has a distinct shade of meaning; CUET tests picking the exact right one

Modals (can, could, may, might, must, should, would, need, dare, used to) all attach to a base verb without "to", and each carries a specific shade of meaning — CUET's distractors are almost always other modals that are grammatically fine but mean something subtly different.

Modals by the meaning they add

ModalCore meaning
can / couldability, permission (could = more polite/past)
may / mightpossibility, formal permission (might = less certain than may)
muststrong obligation, or a confident logical conclusion
should / ought toadvice, mild obligation, expectation
wouldpolite request, habitual past action, conditional result
used toa past habit or state that no longer continues
need (not)necessity, or its absence — 'need not' = 'it isn't necessary to'
dareboldness/challenge — mostly in negatives and questions

Modal + have + past participle — talking about the past

FormMeaning
must have + V3confident conclusion about the past
should have + V3a past action that was advisable but didn't happen — regret/criticism
could have + V3a past ability/possibility that didn't happen
would have + V3the result side of a past unreal condition (third conditional)

Method

  1. Identify what KIND of meaning the sentence needs first — obligation? possibility? a past habit? — then match to the one modal that carries exactly that shade.
  2. For "need", check if the sentence is negative ("need not go") — that's a very different meaning from "needs to go".
  3. For past-referring modals (should have/must have/could have), check whether the sentence is about regret, deduction, or unused ability, and match the modal to that specific sense.

⚠ Common traps

  • 'Used to' confused with 'would' for past habits — both can describe repeated past actions, but only 'used to' can describe a past STATE (used to live there); 'would' cannot.
  • 'Must' (obligation) vs 'must have' (deduction about the past) — same modal, very different job depending on what follows.
  • 'May' and 'can' both offered for permission — 'may' is the more formal/correct choice in a formal-register CUET sentence.
  • 'Need not go' (it isn't necessary) mistaken for 'must not go' (it's forbidden) — opposite meanings, easy to conflate.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Match the exact shade of meaning

'How _____ you shout at your elder sister?' Choose: shall / would / could / must.

1

Notice the tone: a rhetorical, disapproving question about someone's past/ongoing behaviour.

2

'Shall' is for offers/suggestions (shall we?); 'would' is for polite requests or habits; 'must' would demand an answer about obligation, not disapproval.

3

'Could' in this rhetorical-question form expresses disapproving surprise at someone's behaviour — 'how could you'.

Answer: Could — expresses disapproving surprise, the idiomatic 'how could you' pattern.

Method 2 — 'need not' means it's unnecessary

'I have a pen drive so you _____ to the market for purchasing one.' Choose: need not to have gone / need not go / need not going / need not to go.

1

Identify the sense needed: because I already have one, going to the market is unnecessary.

2

'Need' as a modal (not the main verb 'to need') takes the bare infinitive directly, no 'to': 'need not go', not 'need not to go'.

3

Eliminate all three '-ing'/'to'-containing options — none follow the modal grammar of 'need'.

Answer: Need not go — 'need' as a modal takes the bare infinitive, no 'to'.

Method 3 — used to, for a discontinued past habit

'When I was in college I _____ play cricket.' Choose: may / used to / must / dare to.

1

Identify the sense: a repeated action in the past that's implied to no longer happen (given the 'when I was in college' framing).

2

'Used to' is specifically for past habits/states that have since stopped — exactly this sense.

3

'May', 'must', and 'dare to' don't carry the 'this no longer happens' implication at all.

Answer: Used to — the modal specifically for a discontinued past habit.
notes.gr-voice:
≈4 questions per paper — mechanical once you know the by-tense recipe, including the less-obvious imperative and question forms

Passive voice moves the object of an active sentence into the subject position, and adds a form of "be" + past participle. CUET tests the standard recipe across tenses, plus two forms students forget: imperatives and questions.

The recipe, by tense

ActivePassive
Simple present: he writesit is written
Simple past: he wroteit was written
Present continuous: he is writingit is being written
Present perfect: he has writtenit has been written
Future simple: he will writeit will be written
Modal + verb: he can writeit can be written

Two forms students forget

Sentence typePassive form
Imperative (request/command)'You are requested to X' → 'Please X' (an imperative REVERSES back to a direct command when going passive→active)
Question'Why are you making a hole?' → 'Why is a hole being made?' — the auxiliary still inverts with the subject

Method

  1. Find the tense of the active sentence FIRST — the passive must use the exact matching form of "be" for that same tense.
  2. Move the object of the active sentence to the front as the new subject.
  3. Keep the "by + doer" phrase only if the doer is important information; many CUET passive→active conversions expect you to supply a generic "we/they/someone" if the doer was never named.
  4. For questions, keep the question word and the inverted auxiliary — only the main verb's voice changes.

⚠ Common traps

  • Passive tense doesn't match the active sentence's original tense — a very common distractor swaps 'was' for 'has been' or similar.
  • The 'by + doer' phrase kept awkwardly when a natural active sentence wouldn't name a specific doer at all.
  • An imperative's passive→active conversion adding an unnecessary explanation instead of a direct command.
  • In question passives, forgetting to keep the auxiliary inverted with the subject (is it / was it), not just tacking 'being done' onto the end.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Passive imperative back to active

Change to Active Voice: 'You are requested to polish my shoes.' Choose: 'Polish my shoes, please!' / 'It is a request for polishing my shoes' / 'Polish shoes, Please' / 'Please get my shoes polish'.

1

Recognise 'you are requested to' as the passive form of a polite request/imperative.

2

The active-voice equivalent of a passive request is simply the direct imperative itself, softened with 'please'.

3

Reject options that turn it into an abstract noun phrase ('a request for...') — that's not how imperatives convert.

Answer: Polish my shoes, please! — the direct imperative form.

Method 2 — Future tense passive→active

Change to active voice: 'The shipment will be sent by Friday.' Choose: 'By Friday the shipment will be sent by us' / 'We will send the shipment by Friday' / 'We will have sent the shipment by Friday' / 'By Friday the shipment will have been sent'.

1

Identify the tense: simple future passive ('will be sent').

2

The active equivalent needs simple future active, not future perfect — reject options changing the tense to 'will have sent'.

3

Supply a sensible doer since none was named: 'we'.

Answer: We will send the shipment by Friday — simple future active, matching the original tense exactly.

Method 3 — A question in passive voice

Change to Passive Voice: 'Why are you making a hole in the wall?'

1

Identify the object becoming the new subject: 'a hole'.

2

Keep the question word 'why' and the auxiliary inverted with the new subject: 'why is a hole...'

3

Match the tense — present continuous active becomes present continuous passive: 'is being made', not 'was being made'.

Answer: Why is a hole being made in the wall? — question word and inverted auxiliary both preserved.
notes.gr-speech:
≈4 questions per paper — tense backshift, pronoun/time-word changes, and the different reporting verbs for statements/questions/commands

Converting between direct and indirect (reported) speech changes three things together: the tense (usually shifts one step into the past), the pronouns (to match the reporter's point of view), and the time/place words (today→that day, here→there).

Tense backshift

DirectIndirect
simple presentsimple past
simple pastpast perfect
present continuouspast continuous
present perfectpast perfect
willwould
can / maycould / might

Time and place word changes

DirectIndirect
todaythat day
yesterdaythe day before / the previous day
tomorrowthe next day / the following day
nowthen
herethere
thisthat

Reporting verb by sentence type

Direct sentence typeReporting structure
Statementsaid / said that + backshifted clause
Yes/No questionasked / wondered + if/whether + backshifted clause (no auxiliary inversion, no '?')
Wh- questionasked + wh-word + backshifted clause (statement word order, not question order)
Command/requesttold/ordered/requested + object + to-infinitive
Exclamationexclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise that + backshifted clause

Method

  1. Identify the sentence type FIRST (statement / yes-no question / wh-question / command) — each needs a different reporting structure, not just "said that" for everything.
  2. Backshift the tense one full step into the past, unless the direct statement is a universal/timeless truth (those can stay in present tense).
  3. Convert every pronoun and time/place word to match the reporter's perspective, not just the tense.
  4. For questions, switch back to STATEMENT word order inside the reported clause — no auxiliary inversion, no question mark.

⚠ Common traps

  • A reported yes/no question keeping question word order ('asked if did she like it') instead of statement order ('asked if she liked it').
  • A universal truth wrongly backshifted (should stay present: 'said that the sun rises in the east', not 'rose').
  • Reporting verb mismatched to sentence type — 'said' used for what should be 'asked' or 'requested'.
  • 'Said to' kept in indirect speech instead of switching to 'told' (told doesn't take 'to' before the person).

Worked methods

Method 1 — A wondering/exclamatory question to indirect

Convert to indirect: She said, 'How can I do such a work!'

1

Notice this is really an exclamatory rhetorical question, not a plain information-seeking question — 'wondered' fits better than a flat 'asked'.

2

Backshift the modal: can → could.

3

Keep statement word order in the reported clause: 'how she could do such a work', not 'how could she do'.

Answer: She wondered how she could do such a work — captures both the rhetorical tone and the correct backshift/word order.

Method 2 — Simple past backshifts to past perfect

Convert to indirect: Abdul said, 'I saw this film yesterday.'

1

Identify the tense: simple past ('saw') — one step further back is past perfect.

2

Change the pronoun 'I' to 'he' (Abdul), and 'yesterday' to 'the day before'.

3

Assemble: Abdul said that he had seen that film the day before.

Answer: Abdul said that he had seen that film the day before — tense, pronoun, and time-word all converted together.

Method 3 — Reconstructing direct speech from indirect

Convert to direct speech: The judge asked the thief what he had been doing with his hand in the gentleman's pocket.

1

Identify the reporting verb and sentence type: 'asked... what' — a wh-question, reported.

2

Reverse the tense: had been doing (past perfect continuous) shifts forward one step to was doing (past continuous) in direct speech.

3

Restore question word order and a question mark inside the quotation.

Answer: The judge said to the thief, "What were you doing with your hand in the gentleman's pocket?" — tense shifted forward, question order and punctuation restored.
notes.gr-error-detection:
≈4 questions per paper — a sentence split into segments; find which one is wrong, or confirm "No error"

A sentence is broken into 3–4 underlined/labelled segments, one of which may contain a grammar error — plus a "No error" option when the sentence is actually correct. This tests every other grammar topic at once, so it rewards a systematic scan over a single rule.

A checklist to scan, segment by segment

CheckWhat to look for
Subject–verb agreementdoes the segment's verb match its own subject in number?
Tense consistencydoes this segment's tense make sense next to the others?
Prepositionis it the fixed, idiomatic preposition for this verb/adjective?
Article/determinera/an/the present, absent, or wrong where one is needed?
Parallel structureif the sentence lists things, are they in the same grammatical form?
Comparison words'than' used correctly, comparative form matches (more X than Y, not 'more X as Y')

Method

  1. Read the WHOLE sentence once for overall sense before checking any single segment.
  2. Go segment by segment against the checklist above — most errors are one specific, nameable mistake, not a vague "sounds off".
  3. Don't assume there must be an error — "No error" is a genuine, correct answer on a meaningful fraction of these questions; picking a segment just because the sentence sounds slightly formal is a common false positive.
  4. If two segments both seem slightly odd, pick the one with a nameable, rule-based error over one that's just stylistically unusual.

⚠ Common traps

  • Choosing a segment that's just unusual phrasing, when a different segment has the actual rule violation.
  • Missing 'No error' as a real option out of habit, assuming every question must contain a mistake.
  • An error hiding in a short, easy-to-skim segment (a single preposition or article) rather than the longest one.
  • A comparison error — 'more X than Y' malformed as 'more X as Y' or 'more X to Y'.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Scan segment by segment against the checklist

Identify the segment with the error: 'scarcely did I reach the station' / 'nervous and tense than the train sped away' / 'leaving me lonely in a strange place' / 'No error'.

1

Segment 1: correct inverted structure after 'scarcely... when/than' openers.

2

Segment 2: 'nervous and tense than' — 'than' needs a comparison ('more nervous... than'), but there's no comparative structure here at all; this is the broken link connecting the clauses.

3

Segment 3: grammatically fine on its own.

Answer: Nervous and tense than the train sped away — the connector 'than' doesn't fit; the sentence needed 'when', not a comparison word.

Method 2 — Confirming 'No error'

Check for an error: 'I never remember having met a more interesting man in my life.'

1

Check tense: 'never remember having met' is a correct, idiomatic present-tense + perfect-gerund structure.

2

Check the comparative: 'a more interesting man' is correctly formed.

3

Nothing here actually breaks a rule — resist the urge to flag something just because the sentence is a little formal.

Answer: No error — the sentence is grammatically correct as written.

Method 3 — A short-segment error, easy to skim past

Pick the incorrect part: 'The blessings that the habit of reading confers / on their possessor / are many provided we / choose the right kind of books.'

1

Check each short segment individually rather than skimming past the shorter ones.

2

'on their possessor' — 'their' doesn't agree with the singular 'the habit of reading' (or its singular possessor); should be 'its possessor' or 'his/her possessor'.

3

The other three segments are all grammatically sound.

Answer: On their possessor — a pronoun-agreement error hiding in the shortest segment.
notes.gr-sentence-correction:
A small handful of questions per paper — pick the one grammatically correct sentence, sometimes as a multi-select "which are wrong" format

Unlike Error Detection (which shows one sentence, segmented), Sentence Correction shows 3–4 whole, different sentences and asks which is correct — or, in a format that shows up in real papers, gives 4–5 labelled sentences and asks you to identify ALL the incorrect ones together.

Recurring error types across the wrong options

Error typeExample of the mistake
Double comparative/superlative'the seniorest' (already superlative -est, doesn't need 'most' logic either) instead of 'the most senior' or just 'senior to'
Wrong preposition after a fixed verb'discussed about the matter' — 'discuss' never takes 'about'
Wrong preposition of time'sleeping on 3pm' / 'sleeping at 3pm' (a point in time) vs 'sleeping since 3pm' (a duration from that point)
Faulty parallel structure or dangling participle'Having been a rainy day, we cancelled' — a participle needs the SAME subject as the main clause; the day isn't having anything, so this needs 'it being a rainy day' instead
Non-standard phrasing (calques from another language)'what is your good name?' — grammatically odd in standard English despite being common everyday speech

Method

  1. For a 4-way "pick the correct one" question, actively look for the SPECIFIC error in each wrong option — don't just pick whichever "sounds most normal".
  2. For a multi-select "which are incorrect" question, evaluate every labelled sentence independently before combining into a final answer — don't let one obvious error bias your read of the others.
  3. Watch for a dangling modifier at the start of a sentence — the subject of the introductory phrase must match the subject of the main clause.

⚠ Common traps

  • A double superlative/comparative that sounds emphatic but is grammatically redundant ('the seniorest', 'more better').
  • A verb that never takes a preposition in standard usage getting one added anyway ('discussed about').
  • A dangling participle at the sentence's start, describing the wrong subject.
  • A sentence that's common in casual/translated speech but non-standard in formal written English.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Spot the redundant superlative

Identify the correct sentence: 'I am the seniorest to you' / 'I am more senior than you' / 'I am the most senior to you' / 'I am senior to you'.

1

'Seniorest' isn't a real superlative form — 'senior' doesn't take '-est'.

2

'More senior than you' and 'the most senior to you' both misuse comparison words with 'senior', which pairs with 'to', not 'than'/'most... to'.

3

'Senior to you' is the correct, standard comparative pattern for this specific adjective.

Answer: I am senior to you — the correct, standard use of the comparative 'senior to'.

Method 2 — Fixing a dangling participle

Select the correct option: '_____, we had to cancel the trip.' Choose: Being a rainy day / Having been a rainy day / It had been a rainy day / It being a rainy day.

1

Check what the introductory phrase's implied subject is versus the main clause's subject ('we').

2

'Being a rainy day' and 'having been a rainy day' both wrongly imply 'we' were the rainy day — a dangling participle.

3

The day itself needs its own subject 'it' attached to the participle phrase: 'it being a rainy day'.

Answer: It being a rainy day — supplies the correct subject 'it' for the participle phrase, avoiding the dangling-modifier error.

Method 3 — A duration vs point-in-time preposition

Choose the grammatically correct sentence: 'He has been sleeping since 3 pm' / 'for 3 pm' / 'on 3 pm' / 'at 3 pm'.

1

'Has been sleeping' (present perfect continuous) needs a preposition marking the START point of a duration.

2

'Since' is exactly that — a fixed point that a duration is measured FROM ('since 3pm' = starting at 3pm, continuing to now).

3

'For' would need a length of time (for three hours), not a clock time; 'on'/'at' don't fit a continuing duration at all.

Answer: He has been sleeping since 3 pm — 'since' correctly marks the starting point of an ongoing duration.
notes.gr-conditionals:
A small handful of questions per paper — matching the IF-clause and main-clause tenses correctly, mostly the 2nd and 3rd conditional

Each conditional type pairs a SPECIFIC tense in the "if" clause with a SPECIFIC tense in the main clause — CUET's distractors almost always mix tenses from two different conditional types in one sentence.

The four conditional types

TypeIf-clauseMain clauseMeaning
Zerosimple presentsimple presentgeneral/scientific truth — always true
Firstsimple presentwill + base verba real possibility in the future
Secondsimple pastwould + base verban unreal/unlikely present or future situation
Thirdpast perfectwould have + past participlean unreal PAST situation — something that didn't happen

Method

  1. Decide which real-world timeframe the sentence is about: a general truth, a real future possibility, an unlikely present, or an already-closed past.
  2. Match BOTH halves of the sentence to that one conditional type's exact tense pair — a hybrid of two types is always wrong.
  3. For third conditional (talking about the unreal past), watch for "had known/had seen/had done" in the if-clause and "would have + V3" in the main clause, together.

⚠ Common traps

  • Mixing tenses from two conditional types — e.g. simple past in the if-clause with a simple 'would' main clause meant for present, instead of 'would have' for past.
  • A situation clearly about the unreal PAST (something that already didn't happen) answered with second-conditional forms instead of third.
  • A modal other than 'would' substituted in where the specific conditional structure requires 'would'.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Recognising the third conditional (unreal past)

'I didn't know Rahul was in the hospital. If I _____, I would _____ him.' Choose: knew,go / had known,have visited / have known,be going / know,had gone.

1

Note the context: this is about the PAST — a fact ('I didn't know') that's already over and can't be changed.

2

An unreal past situation needs the third conditional: had + past participle in the if-clause, would have + past participle in the main clause.

3

Reject any option using simple past ('knew') — that's second conditional, for a present/future unreal situation, not this past one.

Answer: Had known, have visited — the third-conditional pair, correctly matching the unreal-past context.

Method 2 — Matching both halves consistently

'I did not see you at the party. If I_____you, I surely________to you.' Choose: had saw,spoken / had seen,would have spoken / seen,would speak / had see,would have speak.

1

Confirm this is also third conditional (an unreal past — the party already happened, and I didn't see you).

2

The if-clause needs 'had seen' (correct past participle of 'see') — reject 'had saw' and 'had see', which use the wrong verb form entirely.

3

The main clause needs 'would have spoken', matching third-conditional structure exactly.

Answer: Had seen, would have spoken — the only option with correct third-conditional forms on both sides.

Method 3 — Second conditional with a modal variation

'If I were a cosmonaut, I _____ have taken you to the moon.' Choose: must / would / may / might.

1

Notice 'were' in the if-clause (not 'was') — the classic subjunctive marker for second conditional, regardless of subject.

2

Second conditional's main clause needs 'would' (or would/could/might depending on certainty) + base verb — here 'have taken' needs 'would' specifically to form the standard pattern.

3

'Must' doesn't fit a hypothetical result at all; it signals obligation, not a hypothetical consequence.

Answer: Would — completes the standard second-conditional 'if I were..., I would...' pattern.
notes.gr-question-tags:
≈1–2 questions per paper — a small, fully mechanical rule set. Get every one right.

A question tag flips the polarity of the main statement (positive statement → negative tag, and vice versa) and echoes its auxiliary verb and subject as a pronoun — a handful of special cases cover the rest.

The core rule

Positive statement → negative tag. Negative statement → positive tag.

The tag reuses the sentence's own auxiliary (or a matching form of do/be/have) + a pronoun standing in for the subject.

Special cases CUET tests specifically

Sentence patternTag
Let's + verbshall we?
Imperative (command/request)will you?
I am...aren't I? (not 'am I not' or 'amn't I')
Nothing / Nobody / No one as subjectpositive tag, treated as negative in meaning — 'Nobody called, did they?'
Few / Little (negative in meaning, positive in form)positive tag — 'Few students knew the solution, did they?'
Sentence with no obvious auxiliary (uses a main verb only)borrow 'do/does/did' — 'She cooks well, doesn't she?'

Method

  1. Identify polarity first: does the main clause read as positive or negative overall?
  2. Find the sentence's auxiliary verb (is/has/can/will/etc.) — the tag reuses that SAME auxiliary, not a new one.
  3. If there's no auxiliary (a simple-tense main verb only), the tag borrows do/does/did, matching the main verb's tense.
  4. Convert the subject to its matching pronoun (Your sister → she, the students → they).
  5. Watch for words that are grammatically positive but negative in MEANING (few, little, hardly, scarcely, nobody) — these take a positive tag despite the sentence sounding negative.

⚠ Common traps

  • A tag built from the wrong auxiliary — matching the main verb's meaning instead of its own grammatical auxiliary.
  • 'Few'/'little'/'hardly' treated as needing a negative tag because they FEEL negative — they're grammatically positive and need a positive tag.
  • 'Let's' answered with anything other than the fixed 'shall we?'.
  • 'I am' tagged as 'am I not?' instead of the only standard spoken form, 'aren't I?'.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Borrow do/does when there's no auxiliary

'Your sister cooks well, _____?' Choose: do your / not cooks / doesn't she / doesn't well.

1

Identify the main verb: 'cooks' — simple present, no helper/auxiliary verb present in the sentence.

2

Borrow 'does' (matching simple present, third person singular) since there's no existing auxiliary to reuse.

3

Flip polarity: statement is positive → tag is negative → 'doesn't'.

4

Convert subject 'your sister' to the pronoun 'she'.

Answer: Doesn't she? — borrowed 'does', flipped to negative, subject converted to 'she'.

Method 2 — A grammatically positive but 'negative-feeling' word

'Few students knew the solution, _____.' Choose: were not they? / would not they? / Did they? / do not they?

1

Notice 'few' is grammatically positive in form, even though it feels negative in meaning (almost none knew).

2

A grammatically positive statement takes a NEGATIVE tag by the core rule — but 'few' is treated as already carrying negative force, so the tag stays positive here as the exam convention.

3

Match the tense: 'knew' is simple past, so the tag borrows 'did', not 'were'.

Answer: Did they? — 'few' is treated as inherently negative, so the tag stays positive, and 'did' matches the simple past tense.

Method 3 — The fixed 'Let's' tag

"Let's have a game of cricket, _____?" Choose: don't we? / did we? / shall we? / when?

1

Recognise 'Let's' (let us) as a suggestion, a fixed sentence pattern with its own dedicated tag, not a rule you derive from an auxiliary.

2

The tag for every 'Let's...' sentence is always 'shall we?', regardless of what follows.

Answer: Shall we? — the fixed, memorised tag for every 'Let's...' suggestion.
notes.gr-parts-of-speech:
≈1 question per paper — real papers are dominated by sentence-transformation (assertive ↔ exclamatory), not simple word-class identification

Two things live under this heading: (1) identifying a word's part of speech in a specific sentence, and (2) transforming a sentence from one type to another without changing its meaning — and real CUET papers lean heavily toward the second, especially assertive↔exclamatory conversion.

The eight parts of speech

Noun — namePronoun — replaces a nounVerb — action / state
Adjective — describes a nounAdverb — describes a verb/adj/advPreposition — relation (in, on, of)
Conjunction — joins (and, but, because)Interjection — Oh!, Alas!(articles a/an/the are determiners)

Sentence-type transformation — the real exam skill

ConversionPatternExample
Assertive → ExclamatoryWhat + a/an + adjective + noun (+ subject + verb)! / How + adjective/adverb (+ subject + verb)!'It is a very beautiful evening.' → 'What a beautiful evening it is!'
Exclamatory → AssertiveStrip the exclamation into a plain statement, often with 'very''How kind of you!' → 'It is very kind of you.'
Assertive → InterrogativeInvert the auxiliary, sometimes flipping polarity for a rhetorical question'Everyone loved the movie.' → 'Did everyone not love the movie?'
Affirmative → Negative (same sense)Restate with a double negative or 'no one... did not''Everyone praised him.' → 'There was no one who did not praise him.'

Word-class shifts — the same word, different job

Some CUET questions test that a single word changes its part of speech depending on its role in the sentence — this needs sentence-level reading, not a dictionary lookup.

WordAs one part of speechAs another
fasta fast car (adjective)run fast (adverb) / a day-long fast (noun)
seeingseeing is believing (gerund — a noun)the girl seeing him (present participle — an adjective)
wella well person (adjective, healthy)she sings well (adverb)

Method

  1. For sentence transformation, identify which TYPE conversion is being asked for, then apply its fixed pattern exactly — don't improvise a new phrasing.
  2. For assertive→exclamatory, decide between the "What a/an + noun" pattern (when there's a noun to exclaim about) and the "How + adjective" pattern (when there isn't).
  3. For identifying a word's part of speech, check its JOB in this exact sentence, not its most familiar meaning.
  4. For a gerund vs a participle (both end in -ing), check whether the -ing word is acting as a NOUN (gerund, can be a subject/object) or as an ADJECTIVE describing another noun (participle).

⚠ Common traps

  • 'What' and 'How' exclamatory patterns swapped — 'What' needs a noun after the adjective, 'How' doesn't.
  • A gerund (functions as a noun) confused with a present participle (functions as an adjective) just because both end in -ing.
  • An affirmative→negative transform that accidentally changes the sentence's actual meaning instead of just its grammatical form.
  • A word's most common part of speech assumed, ignoring its actual grammatical job in this specific sentence.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Identify the word's job in this exact sentence

'They fast on Mondays.' What part of speech is 'fast' here?

1

Ignore the word's most common meaning (adjective, 'quick') for a moment.

2

Check what role it plays in this sentence — it's the main action: 'they [do what] on Mondays'.

3

A word performing the action of the sentence is a verb.

Answer: Verb — here 'fast' means 'to go without food', the sentence's main action.

Method 2 — Building the exclamatory transform

Convert to exclamatory: 'It is a very difficult question.'

1

Identify the noun phrase carrying the quality: 'a difficult question'.

2

Use the pattern: What + a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!

3

Assemble: What + a + difficult + question + it + is!

Answer: What a difficult question it is!

Method 3 — Identifying a gerund among lookalikes

Which of the following can be called a gerund? 'Stop playing' / 'I love to go hunting' / 'Kids are sleeping' / 'Seeing is believing'.

1

Check each -ing word's job: 'playing' in 'stop playing' is the object of 'stop' — actually a gerund too, but let's check the others.

2

'Sleeping' in 'kids are sleeping' is part of the continuous verb tense, not a gerund at all.

3

'Seeing' in 'seeing is believing' is the SUBJECT of the sentence — a noun-like role, the clearest gerund use, paired with 'believing' also acting as a noun (complement).

Answer: Seeing is believing — both 'seeing' and 'believing' function as nouns (subject and complement), the clearest gerund use among the options.
notes.gr-literary-devices:
≈2 questions per paper — name the figure of speech, often via a List I/List II match, sometimes inside a poem extract

CUET tests literary devices two ways: naming the device used in a given line, and matching devices to their definitions in a List I/List II format. The device list barely varies year to year — memorise the core set cold.

The core device list

DeviceOne-line testExample
Similecomparison using like / asbrave as a lion
Metaphordirect comparison, no like/ashe is the Einstein of my class
Personificationa non-human thing acts humandeath lays his icy hand on kings
Oxymorontwo contradictory words forced togetherfaith unfaithful kept him falsely true
Hyperboledeliberate, obvious exaggerationI could eat a horse
Alliterationsame consonant sound starts nearby wordsshe sells seashells
Ironythe opposite of what's literally said/expectedcalling a very unlucky day 'a lucky one'
Apostropheaddressing something absent/abstract/non-human directlyO Death, where is thy sting?
Metonymysubstituting a closely-associated thing for the thing itself'the crown' for the monarchy
Onomatopoeiaa word that imitates the sound it describesbuzz, hiss, clang

A real CUET match-the-list question

Match: Metaphor / Personification / Hyperbole / Oxymoron — with — giving human qualities to non-human things / a phrase combining contradictory words / an imaginative comparison without like-as / an exaggerated statement not meant literally.

Real CUET answer pairing (deliberately scrambled in the original options to test if you match by definition, not by guessing order): Personification → gives human qualities; the other three follow the same one-to-one logic.

Method

  1. Find the two things being connected or contrasted in the line — that's the raw material for naming the device.
  2. Check for the literal word "like" or "as" first — its presence or absence is the single fastest simile-vs-metaphor test.
  3. Ask "is a non-human thing doing something only a person/animal can do?" — that's personification, distinct from a metaphor (which just equates two things without action).
  4. For match-list questions, pair the ONE you're most confident about first — with only 4 items, one certain pair eliminates two wrong combinations immediately.

⚠ Common traps

  • Personification mistaken for metaphor — if a thing is DOING a human action, it's personification, not just a comparison.
  • Oxymoron confused with irony — oxymoron is a contradiction packed into one short phrase; irony is a larger situational or verbal reversal.
  • Metaphor and simile with the 'like/as' test skipped, guessed from vibe instead.
  • Match-list options deliberately scrambled so that a plausible-but-wrong pairing sits right next to the correct one.

Worked methods

Method 1 — Personification vs metaphor

Identify the figure of speech: 'Death lays his icy hand on kings.'

1

Check: is Death (non-human, abstract) doing something only a person can do? Yes — 'lays his hand', a human action.

2

This rules out simple metaphor (which would just equate Death with something else, no action) in favour of personification.

Answer: Personification — Death is given the human action of laying a hand.

Method 2 — Spotting an oxymoron

Identify the figure of speech: 'And faith unfaithful kept him falsely true.'

1

Look for two directly contradictory words forced together: 'faith' and 'unfaithful'; 'falsely' and 'true'.

2

Two such contradictions packed into one short line is the signature of an oxymoron, not irony (which needs a larger situational reversal) or personification (no human action here).

Answer: Oxymoron — 'faith unfaithful' and 'falsely true' are both direct word-level contradictions.

Method 3 — Matching devices to definitions under time pressure

Match List I with List II: Metaphor / Personification / Hyperbole / Oxymoron — with the four definitions above.

1

Start with the one you're most sure of: Oxymoron = 'a phrase combining contradictory words' — a clean, unambiguous match.

2

That single confirmed pair removes two of the four wrong combination-options outright.

3

Match the rest by elimination: Personification = human qualities to non-human things; Hyperbole = exaggerated, not literal; Metaphor = imaginative comparison, no like/as.

Answer: Metaphor–comparison, Personification–human qualities, Hyperbole–exaggeration, Oxymoron–contradiction — matched by starting from the most certain pair.

gr-adj-adv.q: Fill in the blanks with the most appropriate adverbs. Does she sing well? _____ she does

gr-adj-adv.q: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate adverb from the given options : He ________ talks ill of his friends.

gr-adj-adv.q: Identify the kind of adverbs in the following sentence : Things are no better at present.

gr-speech.q: Change the following sentence into the Indirect speech by choosing the appropriate option :- Abdul said, "I saw this film yesterday".
opts: Abdul said that he seen this film the day before
Abdul said that he had seen that film the day before
Abdul said that he have seen that film the yesterday
Abdul said that you had seen that film the day before
gr-speech.explain: Simple past ('saw') shifts to past perfect ('had seen') in reported speech, 'this' shifts to 'that', and 'yesterday' shifts to 'the day before' — matching option (B).

gr-speech.q: Change the following into the Direct Speech : - The Management suggested to the Principal that they should wait and watch. Choose the appropriate option from below :-
opts: The Management suggested to the Principal, "wait and watch"
The Management said to the Principal , "Let us wait and watch"
The Management said to the Principal, "Can you wait and watch" ?
The Management said to the Principal, "What a wait and watch,"
gr-speech.explain: A suggestion using 'should' in reported speech converts to direct speech using 'Let us...' to express the same collective suggestion.

gr-speech.q: Choose the appropriate option of Indirect sentence for the sentence given below:- He said, "I shall be there with Sudha soon." A. He said that he will be there with Sudha soon. B. He informed that he would be ne there with Sudha soon. C. He said that Sudha would be there with him soon. D. He said that he had been with Sudha soon. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
gr-speech.explain: 'Shall' shifts to 'would' in reported speech following the past-tense reporting verb 'said': 'he would be there with Sudha soon' — matching (B) (which contains a stray typo 'ne' in the source, but is otherwise the correct conversion).

gr-speech.q: Choose the best option of indirect speech for the sentence given:- Sanjeev said, "I bought a saree for my mother." A. Sanjeev said that he had bought a saree for his mother. B. Sanjeev said that he was buying a saree for his mother. C. Sanjeev said that he had been buying a saree for his mother. D. Sanjeev said that he will be buy a saree for his mother. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
gr-speech.explain: Simple past ('bought') shifts to past perfect ('had bought') in reported speech, matching option (A).

gr-speech.q: Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech. She asked me if I was going to college.
opts: She asked me, "Will you go to college ?"
She said to me "Are you going to college ?"
She asked to me, "Was I going to college ?"
She said, "Am I going to college ?"
gr-speech.explain: This is a reverse conversion (indirect to direct): the reported yes/no question 'if I was going' converts to the direct present continuous question: 'Are you going to college?'

gr-speech.q: Choose the most appropriate option which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech. He said, "Sita, when is the next train ?"
opts: He said to Sita when the next train was
He asked Sita when the next train was
He asked Sita about the next train
He asked when the next train is
gr-speech.explain: A direct question addressed to a named person converts to indirect speech using 'asked + person + question word', with the tense shifted back: 'He asked Sita when the next train was.'

gr-speech.q: Choose the correct form of reported verb when the following sentence is changed to indirect speech: She says, "I enjoy walking".
gr-speech.explain: Since the reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense, the tense of the reported clause is retained, and the pronoun 'I' shifts to 'she': 'She enjoys.'

gr-speech.q: Choose the correct form of reported speech from the options given below: Rakesh said, "Shall I play the movie?"
opts: Rakesh said if he could play the movie?
Rakesh asked that he should play the movie
Rakesh said if he should play the movie
Rakesh asked if he should play the movie
gr-speech.explain: A question with 'Shall I...?' (seeking suggestion/permission) is reported using 'asked if he should...': 'Rakesh asked if he should play the movie.'

gr-speech.q: Choose the correct Indirect form of the following sentence from the given options: She said, "How can I do such a work!"
opts: She asked that how she can do such a work
She said that she can do such a work
She wondered how she could do such a work
She wondered if how she could do such a work
gr-speech.explain: An exclamatory rhetorical question like 'How can I do such a work!' is best reported using 'wondered', with the modal backshifted to 'could': 'She wondered how she could do such a work.'

gr-speech.q: Choose the correct option to change the following sentence into Direct Speech: 'The supervisor confirmed that the office memo was an original one.'
opts: The supervisor said, "the office memo is an original one."
The supervisor said, "the office order was an original one."
The supervisor said, "the office order has been an original one."
The supervisor said, "the office order is an original one."
gr-speech.explain: Converting reported to direct speech removes the backshift: past tense 'was' in the reported clause becomes present tense 'is' in the direct quote, and the noun 'office memo' is retained as originally stated: 'the office memo is an original one.'

gr-speech.q: Identify the correct conversion of the following sentence in Direct Speech into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "What are you doing?"
opts: She said to me what I was doing
She asked me what was I to do
She asked me what I was doing
She told me what I was doing
gr-speech.explain: A direct wh-question converts to indirect speech using 'asked' with normal (non-inverted) word order and the tense shifted back: 'She asked me what I was doing.'

gr-speech.q: Identify the correct conversion of the following sentence in Indirect Speech into Direct Speech: He requested him to wait there till he returned.
opts: He requested to him, 'Please wait there till I return.'
He said to him, 'Please wait here till I return.'
He requested to him, 'Please wait till I return.'
He said to him, 'Please wait there till I return.'
gr-speech.explain: Reported 'there' shifts back to 'here' in direct speech (since the speaker is now physically present at the location), and the reporting verb becomes 'said to' with a polite imperative: 'Please wait here till I return.'

gr-speech.q: Change the following sentence into an Indirect Speech: The teacher said, "Do your work with dedication."
opts: I am advised to do my work with dedication
The teacher advised him to do his work with dedication
I was advised to do his work with dedication
The teacher ordered me to do his work with dedication
gr-speech.explain: An imperative sentence is reported using 'advised/told + object + to-infinitive', with pronouns shifted accordingly: 'The teacher advised him to do his work with dedication.'

gr-speech.q: Change the following sentence into Indirect Speech: I said to my brother, "Don't tell a lie."
opts: I advised my brother not to tell a lie
I asked my brother to not lie
I inspired my brother to tell the truth
I informed my brother to never tell a lie
gr-speech.explain: A negative imperative is reported using 'advised/told + object + not to + infinitive': 'I advised my brother not to tell a lie.'

gr-speech.q: Choose the correct option to change the following sentence into Direct Speech: He commanded me to guard the door.
gr-speech.explain: In direct speech, an imperative command uses the imperative base form of the verb inside quotes preceded by the reporting verb 'said': He said, "Guard the door."

gr-speech.q: Change the following statement to direct speech : He asked me what I wanted.
opts: He said to me, "What I want?"
He said to me, "What do you want ?"
He said to me, "What he wants ?"
He said to me, "What will you want ?"
gr-speech.explain: Reported past tense 'wanted' converts back to the present tense question form in direct speech, with the pronoun restored to 'you': 'What do you want?'

gr-speech.q: Choose the option which best expresses the given sentence in indirect speech : I said to Bob, "Can you complete this work by tomorrow ?"
opts: I asked Bob whether he could complete this work by the next day ?
I asked Bob whether he could complete this work by tomorrow
I asked Bob whether he could complete that work by the next day
I asked Bob whether he could complete that work by the next day ?
gr-speech.explain: Reported yes/no questions use 'whether' with the modal shifted to past ('could'), 'this' shifts to 'that', 'tomorrow' shifts to 'the next day', and reported speech ends as a statement, not a question — matching option (C).

gr-speech.q: Choose the option to correctly change the following from direct to indirect speech. "Are you free tomorrow ?" She said to me.
opts: She told me are you free tomorrow
She asked me if I was free tomorrow
She asked me if I was free the next day
She ordered and asked if I was free tomorrow
gr-speech.explain: A reported yes/no question uses 'if/whether' with the tense shifted to past ('was'), and 'tomorrow' shifts to 'the next day.'

gr-speech.q: Select the appropriate option as the conversion for the following statement into indirect speech. - Fiona said, "It's getting late" -
opts: Fiona said it meant to be late
Fiona said it had been late
Fiona said it has been getting late
Fiona said that it was getting late
gr-speech.explain: Present continuous ('is getting') shifts to past continuous ('was getting') in reported speech: 'Fiona said that it was getting late.'
