gr-error-detection.explain: With 'no sooner... than' constructions, the auxiliary verb must be inverted with the subject: it should read 'No sooner had she realized', making the given phrase 'No sooner she had realized' the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the part of a sentence that is grammatically incorrect
opts: in India is how AI can be a
gr-error-detection.explain: After the preposition 'by', a gerund is required, not the base verb: it should read 'by bridging the digital divide', making the final segment the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the part of the following sentence that contains an error : Ranjeeta does not usually prefer staying at cottages, but last winter she spent few days in one.
opts: She spent few days into one
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Spent... into one' should be 'spent... in one' — the incorrect preposition 'into' makes the final segment the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the part of the following sentence that contains an error : The most important feature of our products are that they are all created by hand.
gr-error-detection.explain: The singular subject 'feature' requires the singular verb 'is', not 'are' — making the segment 'of our products are that' the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the part of the following sentence that contains an error : If a company sends its employees abroad to work for a foreign client, they pays them a daily allowance.
opts: To work for a foreign client, they
gr-error-detection.explain: The subject 'they' (referring to 'a company') requires the plural verb 'pay', not 'pays' — making the final segment the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the part of the following sentence that contains an error : It is the quarter to ten by my watch.
gr-error-detection.explain: Expressions of time like 'quarter to ten' do not take the definite article 'the' — it should simply be 'It is quarter to ten,' making the first segment the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Spot the error in the following sentence It is often said that some men are born great, some achieve greatness and some had greatness threst on them.
opts: some had greatness threst on them
gr-error-detection.explain: To match the parallel present-tense structure ('are born', 'achieve'), the final clause should read 'some have greatness thrust upon them', not 'had... threst' — making the last segment the error (also containing the misspelling 'threst' for 'thrust').

gr-error-detection.q: The given sentence is divided into three parts. Scan it carefully for errors and choose the most appropriate options A) I found less | B) books in the | C) library than that
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Less' should be 'fewer' since 'books' is a countable plural noun — making part (A) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: The given sentence is divided into three parts. Read each part carefully for errors and choose the most appropriate option. A) Few persons B) are free C) from worries
gr-error-detection.explain: The sentence 'Few persons are free from worries' is grammatically correct throughout, with no errors.

gr-error-detection.q: Read the following sentence care. Some part of the sentence may have an error. Choose the most appropriate options. Mumbai (A) | is New York (B) | of India (C)
gr-error-detection.explain: Comparing Mumbai to New York should use 'the New York' — the missing article before 'New York' makes part (B) contain the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error:
opts: scarcely did I reach the station
nervous and tense than the train sped away
leaving me lonely in a strange place
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Scarcely... than' is incorrect; 'scarcely' should be paired with 'when', not 'than' — making the second segment the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error:
opts: your short story should feature a protagonist
as self discovery of some kind
gr-error-detection.explain: The singular antecedent 'a challenging situation' requires a singular verb in the relative clause: 'which results' instead of 'which result'.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the option(s) that is/are the incorrect part of the sentence given below.
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Majority of people' is a plural subject and requires the plural verb 'prefer', not 'prefers' — making part (B) the grammatical error.

gr-error-detection.q: The sentence given below is in parts. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
opts: the father went to the edge of the steep hill
and called out repeatedly to his son
but receives no answer Choose the correct answer from the options given below
gr-error-detection.explain: The sentence is in the simple past tense throughout ('went', 'called out'), so 'receives' in part (D) breaks tense consistency and should be 'received' — making (D) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Spot the Error in the sentence : My sister-in-law who lives in Mumbai have, come to stay with us
gr-error-detection.explain: The singular subject 'My sister-in-law' requires the singular verb 'has come', not 'have come' — making part (C) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Find out which part of the sentence has an error ? Choose the correct option : Supposing if it rains, what shall we do ?
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Supposing' and 'if' both introduce a conditional and shouldn't be used together — using both is redundant, making 'supposing if' the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Choose the option without an error :-
opts: The love is the beautiful emotion
The love is a natural emotion
gr-error-detection.explain: Abstract nouns like 'love' used generically take no article: 'Love is a beautiful emotion' is correct, while the other options wrongly add 'the' before 'love.'

gr-error-detection.q: Spot the error in the sentence : - Although I am playing cricket for more than three years, I have not been able to score a century.
gr-error-detection.explain: An action continuing from the past into the present ('for more than three years') requires the present perfect continuous tense, not present continuous — so 'I am playing' should be 'I have been playing', making part (A) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Read the sentence to find out if there is an error and choose the corresponding answer A. The solution B. which he provided C. does not hint the D. possibility of E. an alternative answer Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Hint the possibility' is an incorrect phrasal construction; it should be 'hint AT the possibility' — making segment (C) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Read the sentence to find out if there is an error and choose the corresponding answer A. Climatic shifts are B. so gradual they can be C. indistinguishable at first D. from ordinary fluctuations E. in the weather Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
gr-error-detection.explain: The comparative 'so gradual... they can be' is missing the correlative 'that' commonly required with 'so... that' constructions, making segment (B) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Which one of the given sentences is not grammatically correct?
opts: She came while the meeting was over
This is the house where I lived for ten years
The doctor discharged the patient from the hospital
gr-error-detection.explain: 'While' should not be used with a completed action like 'was over'; the correct conjunction would be 'after' — making this sentence incorrect.

gr-error-detection.q: My uncle is enough rich to buy a car.

My uncle is richer enough to buy a car
My uncle in enough richer to buy a car
gr-error-detection.explain: 'Enough' follows the adjective it modifies, not precedes it: 'rich enough', not 'enough rich.'

gr-error-detection.q: Identify the part of the sentence which has an error.
gr-error-detection.explain: In standard English, one 'turns on' or 'switches on' a light, not 'opens' it — 'to open the light' is an incorrect usage, making part (C) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Identify the part of the sentence which has an error:

gr-error-detection.q: The following sentence is grammatically incorrect: A great person use to lived in this house. Correct the sentence above by choosing the most appropriate option:
opts: A great person lived to use in that house
A great person used to lived in that house
A great person used to live in this house

gr-error-detection.explain: 'Used to' is followed by the base form of the verb: 'used to live', not 'use to lived' — matching option (C), which also correctly keeps 'this house' matching the original sentence.

gr-error-detection.explain: The correct phrasing is 'made up of firewood', not 'on fire wood' — the wrong preposition and split spelling make part (E) the error.

gr-error-detection.q: Pick the incorrect part in the given sentence. The blessings that the habit of reading confers/on their possessor/are many provided we/choose the right kind of books.

choose the right kind of books

gr-sentence-correction.q: Select the correct option to make a grammatically correct sentence: _____, we had to cancel the trip.

gr-sentence-correction.explain: To avoid a dangling participle, the dummy subject 'It' is required before the participle clause when referring to weather: 'It being a rainy day...'

gr-sentence-correction.q: Select the incorrect sentences from the following options: A. The roof collapsed that very moment. B. This is more than flesh and blood can endure. C. He puts on an air of dignity. D. The tailor's bill has hurried up to a large amount. E. They were very grateful to him for kindness. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
gr-sentence-correction.explain: (D) 'hurried up to a large amount' should be 'mounted/run up to a large amount', and (E) is missing an article ('for his kindness'); the source's key also flags (A), while B and C are treated as standard, correct idiomatic expressions.

gr-sentence-correction.q: Select the incorrect sentences from the following options: A. We discussed about the matter yesterday. B. It is not likely that he will see his home again. C. I would rather you went through air. D. The negotiations were rattled off in secret. E. He urged them to be quiet and listen to his words. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
gr-sentence-correction.explain: 'Discussed about' is redundant — 'discuss' already means 'talk about' (A wrong); 'went through air' is a garbled phrase, likely meant to be 'went by air' (C wrong); 'rattled off' means said quickly, which doesn't fit 'in secret' — negotiations would be 'carried on/conducted in secret' (D wrong).

gr-sentence-correction.q: Choose the grammatically correct sentences from the following options given:
opts: Indian equities surged to fresh records on Wednesday
Desire is never satisfied by the enjoyment of the objects of desire
Mankind was stemmed from one root, though it is split up into different communities
gr-sentence-correction.explain: (B), (C) and (E) are standard, grammatically sound sentences. (A) 'What is your good name?' is a non-standard construction not used in formal English, and (D) 'was stemmed from' is an awkward, non-standard phrasing.

gr-sentence-correction.q: Identify the correct sentence/s from the following:
opts: I am the seniorest to you
I am more senior than you
I am the most senior to you
gr-sentence-correction.explain: Latin comparative adjectives such as senior, junior, superior, and inferior take the preposition 'to' (not 'than') and do not take comparative markers like 'more' or '-est'. Only statement (D) is correct.

gr-conditionals.q: Choose the correct option to fill in the blank with the appropriate modal in the following sentence : If I were a cosmonaut, I _____ have taken you to the moon :
gr-conditionals.explain: This is a second conditional (hypothetical present) sentence, which takes 'would have' in the main clause.

gr-conditionals.q: Choose the appropriate word pair to complete the sentence: I didn't know Rahul was in the hospital. If I ________, I would ________ him.'
gr-conditionals.explain: This is a third conditional (referring to an unreal past situation) — requiring 'had known' (past perfect) in the if-clause and 'would have visited' (perfect conditional) in the main clause.

gr-question-tags.q: Fill in the blank with a suitable 'Question Tag' for the given sentence: The scuba divers need air cylinders, _______
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive statement using the main verb 'need' (not as a modal) takes a negative question tag with 'do/don't': 'don't they?'

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the appropriate question tag for the following sentence out of the options given below : Let's have a game of cricket.
gr-question-tags.explain: Sentences beginning with 'Let's' (suggestions) always take the question tag 'shall we?'

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the correct question tag ?
opts: She didn't do that, didn't she ?
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive statement in the simple past ('said') takes a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary 'did': 'He said that, didn't he?'

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the correct question tag for the following sentence : You are a real piece of work, _________ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive present-tense statement with 'are' takes the negative question tag 'aren't you?'

gr-question-tags.q: Select the appropriate question tag for the given sentence: It looks perfect here.
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive sentence in Simple Present ('looks') requires a negative auxiliary tag using 'does': 'doesn't it?'

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the suitable question tag from the options given below : Your sister cooks well, ________ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive statement in the present simple ('cooks') takes a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary and pronoun: 'doesn't she?'

gr-question-tags.q: Add a question tag to the following sentence by choosing the appropriate one : - It's very hot today, _________ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive statement ('It's very hot') takes a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary 'is': 'Isn't it?'

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the appropriate question tag from the given options to complete the given sentence Most of us will join the party, ________ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: The main clause uses the future modal 'will', so the question tag must match with 'won't we?'

gr-question-tags.q: Have some more rice, _______ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: Imperative sentences (offers/requests) take the question tag 'will you?' regardless of the imperative's implied subject.

gr-question-tags.q: Use the correct Question tag for the given sentence: I am always on time, _______ ?
gr-question-tags.explain: The subject 'I' with 'am' irregularly takes the question tag 'aren't I?' in standard English.

gr-question-tags.q: Choose the most suitable question tag for the following phrase: 'They will solve it.'
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive statement using the auxiliary 'will' takes a negative question tag with the same auxiliary: 'They will solve it, won't they?'

gr-question-tags.q: Fill in the blank with an appropriate Question Tag: You think this is funny, ______?
gr-question-tags.explain: The main verb 'think' (not an auxiliary) requires the auxiliary 'do' in the question tag: 'do you?'

gr-question-tags.q: Complete the following sentence by using a suitable question tag: 'Few students knew the solution, _________.'
gr-question-tags.explain: 'Few' functions as a negative quantifier (implying 'not many'), so the main clause is treated as negative and takes a positive question tag using the matching auxiliary 'did': 'Few students knew the solution, did they?'

gr-question-tags.q: Complete the following sentence by using a question tag : I am older to you _________.
gr-question-tags.explain: The subject 'I' with 'am' takes the irregular question tag 'aren't I?' in standard English.

gr-question-tags.q: Add a suitable question tag to the following sentence from the options given below : Mohit lives in the city.
gr-question-tags.explain: A positive present-simple statement takes a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary: 'Doesn't he?'

gr-parts-of-speech.q: Choose the correct form of the Assertive sentence for the following Exclamatory sentence: If only I were young again!
opts: I wished I were young again
I wish I were young again
I had wished I were young again
gr-parts-of-speech.explain: 'If only...' expressing a present wish converts to the assertive form 'I wish I were young again' (present tense 'wish' matching the unfulfilled present wish).

gr-parts-of-speech.q: Choose the correct option to change the following assertive sentence into an exclamatory sentence : It is a matter of great happiness that we have won the trophy.
opts: Hurrah! we have won the trophy
Alas! we have won the trophy
Hay! we had won the trophy!
gr-parts-of-speech.explain: 'Hurrah!' conveys joy/celebration, and the present perfect tense 'have won' is preserved from the original: 'Hurrah! we have won the trophy.'

gr-parts-of-speech.q: Identify the exclamatory sentence :
opts: Talking much is a sign of vanity
What a beautiful dress she is wearing
My views do not appeal to him. Choose the correct answer from the options given below
gr-parts-of-speech.explain: 'What a beautiful dress she is wearing' follows the 'What a(n) + adjective + noun + subject + verb' exclamatory pattern, expressing admiration.

gr-parts-of-speech.q: Which of the following can be called Gerund :
gr-parts-of-speech.explain: 'Playing' (A, object of 'stop'), 'hunting' (B, object of 'go'), and 'Seeing'/'believing' (D, functioning as subject and complement) are all gerunds (verb+ing used as nouns); 'sleeping' (C) and 'smoking' (E) are present participles forming continuous tense, not gerunds.

gr-literary-devices.q: In stark contrast to where I grew up-in warm, lush green Trivandrum, Kerala, filled with rich sights, sounds and people-life at the Poles is quiet. The harshness of winter brings along with it an eerie desolation and near-total silence. Survival in this frigid, dark and windy terrain is only for the fittest. A misstep can mean anything from an icy injury to a bitter, benumbed death. But while it is tenuous, life here is also humbling-physically, mentally, and even spiritually. The experience has allowed me to witness the wonderous dualities of nature: raw, brutal and unforgiving but nurturing and awe-inspiring at the same time. As the days shorten, almost all life starts to depart seeking warmer lands. But those who stay are surrounded by glacial beauty and an otherworldly stillness that stands unmatched. In peak winter months, the sun seems to live only in memory. Its absence however, is only an illusion: shimmering displays of blue, red, yellow, green, and orange auroras shifting and snaking like billowing curtains across the pitch black sky remind me that the light shall one day return. Even the emptiness of the land is deceptive. Look closely and out waddles a flock of penguins from behind an ice shelf on the Antarctic peninsula. Identify the literary device in the sentence given below: "shimmering displays of blue, red, yellow, green, and orange auroras shifting and snaking like billowing curtains across the pitch black sky..." Choose the correct option:-
gr-literary-devices.explain: The auroras are explicitly compared to curtains using 'like' ('snaking like billowing curtains'), making this a simile.

gr-literary-devices.q: Winter is cold, with gusts of tumbling snow, When rain falls down and nothing ever grows. For children, it's the snow that they desire And cups of cocoa in front of the fire. When winter's gone, the grass grows green again. Roses and tulips sprout with bright green stems. The bees are buzzing, the birds are singing. Sheep are grazing and cow bells are ringing. And then the sun starts to shine too brightly. It's so hot that fans are put on nightly, And so then it's off to the beach or pools Where people swim about just to keep cool. All the leaves on the trees turn golden-brown, And when on the ground make a crackly sound. In autumn a lot of money you make From clearing backyards of leaves with a rake. Each season has its own goods and its bads, But since they are all different I am glad! Identify the poetic device in : "The bees are buzzing ......" Choose the correct option :
gr-literary-devices.explain: 'Buzzing' imitates the actual sound bees make, which is the defining feature of onomatopoeia.

gr-literary-devices.q: Learning the Queen's English is like scrubbing off the bright red varnish from your toe nails, the morning after a dance. It takes a long time and there is always a little bit left at the end, a stain of red along the growing edges to remind you of the good time you had. So, you can see that learning came slowly to me. On the other hand, I had plenty of time. I learned your language in an immigration detention centre, in Essex, in the southeastern part of the United Kingdom. Two years, they locked me in there. Time was all I had. But why did I go to all the trouble ? It is because of what some of the older girls explained to me: to survive, you must look good or talk even better. The plain ones and the silent ones, it seems their paperwork in never in order. You say, they get repatriated. We say, sent home early. The Other Hand is the story of a young woman who flees conflict in her home village in the oil-rich region of southern Nigeria. She makes her way to the UK as an illegal immigrant and is detained for a long period of time at an immigrant detention centre near London. When she finally gets out, she seeks out the only two people she knows in England, whom she met on a Nigerian beach during a life-changing event a few years before. Will she be able to find them, and if so will they help her ? And if not, will she survive in her newly adopted country as an immigrant ? Learning Queen's English is described using a metaphor which is :
opts: a stain of red along the greasing edges
scrubbing off the bright red varnish from your toenails
gr-literary-devices.explain: The passage opens with the comparison: 'Learning the Queen's English is like scrubbing off the bright red varnish from your toe nails.'

gr-literary-devices.q: The waves beside them danced; but they Out-did the sparkling waves in glee: A poet could not but be gay, In such a jocund company: I gazed—and gazed—but little thought What wealth the show to me had brought: For oft, when on my couch I lie In vacant or in pensive mood, They flash upon that inward eye Which is the bliss of solitude; And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the daffodils. Point out the figure of speech in the following line: "I gazed—and gazed"
gr-literary-devices.explain: The word 'gazed' is repeated back-to-back for emphasis, which is the figure of speech known as repetition — there is no exaggeration (hyperbole), contradictory terms (oxymoron), or explicit comparison using 'like/as' (simile).

gr-literary-devices.q: LOVE AND A QUESTION A STRANGER came to the door at eve, And he spoke the bridegroom fair. He bore a green-white stick in his hand, And, for all burden, care. He asked with the eyes more than the lips For a shelter for the night, And he turned and looked at the road afar Without a window light. The bridegroom came forth into the porch With "Let us look at the sky, And question what of the night to be, Stranger, you and I." The woodbine leaves littered the yard, The woodbine berries were blue, Autumn, yes, winter was in the wind; "Stranger, I wish I knew." Within, the bride in the dusk alone Bent over the open fire, Her face rose-red with the glowing coal And the thought of the heart's desire. The bridegroom looked at the weary road, Yet saw but her within, And wished her heart in a case of gold And pinned with a silver pin. The bridegroom thought it little to give a dole of bread, a purse, A heartfelt prayer for the poor of God, Or for the rich a curse, But whether or not a man was asked To mar the love of two By harboring woe in the bridal house, The bridegroom wished he knew. The phrase 'weary road' is an example of :
gr-literary-devices.explain: The tiredness actually belongs to the traveller on the road, not the road itself — transferring the quality 'weary' onto 'road' makes this a transferred epithet.

'He ______ here since Monday.'
'While I ______ dinner, the phone rang.'

gr-tenses.q: 'When it ______ raining, we will start the match.'

gr-articles.q: 'She goes to ______ school by ______ bus.'

gr-articles.q: 'I waited for ______ hour before ______ MP arrived.'

gr-prepositions.q: 'She has invested all her savings ______ property.'

The teacher told the moon revolves

cheat:
Grammar — one-page revision

The split (avg per paper)

Grammar is only ≈8.5 of 50. Biggest: Prepositions ≈1.3 · Literary Devices ≈1.0 · Tenses ≈0.8 · Modals/Error-Detection/Voice/Speech ≈0.6–0.7 each. SVA, Pronouns, Conditionals, Sentence Correction are rare — a quick refresh is enough.

Prepositions (collocations — no rule, just know them)

invest in · depend on · consist of · afraid of · good at · married to · superior to · indistinguishable from · comply with · congratulate on · accuse of. No preposition after discuss, enter, marry, resemble. "different from".

Tenses

Earlier of two past events → past perfect (by the time, before, after). since + point → present/past perfect, never past simple. Future time clause (when/after) → present tense.

Voice

Passive = object→subject + be + V3 (+ by-doer). Continuous → being + V3. Perfect → been + V3. Imperative → "Let + object + be + V3".

Reported speech

Backshift: is→was, has→had, will→would, can→could, V1→V2, V2→had+V3. now→then, today→that day, tomorrow→next day, here→there, this→that. Question → asked if/wh- + statement word order. Command → told/asked + object + to + verb. No backshift for universal truths.

SVA quick rules

Ignore words between subject and verb. along with / as well as → agree with first subject. either…or / neither…nor → agree with nearer subject. each / every / one of → singular. "a number of" → plural; "the number of" → singular.

Conditionals

T1: if + present, will + V1. T2: if + past, would + V1 (use were for all persons). T3: if + past perfect, would have + V3. Never "would" in the if-clause.

Question tags

positive statement → negative tag (and vice-versa), same auxiliary. Negative-meaning words (never, hardly, nobody) → positive tag. "I am" → aren't I?. "Let's" → shall we?

Modals

must not = forbidden ≠ need not = not required. must (deduction) = near-certain. should have + V3 = past regret/criticism. bare infinitive after every modal.

Articles

a/an by sound (an hour, a university, an MP). "the" for unique/superlative/rivers/ranges. No article for abstract or plural nouns used generally, meals, languages, "go to school/bed".
